messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rodrigo is a 58-year-old forensic analyst of Colombian descent who has been married for nearly three decades and has spent the better part of his career examining physical evidence in the service of criminal justice. He presents now with a PCL-5 score of 43, referred by his primary care physician after a routine appointment revealed what his doctor described as "significant stress-related physical findings." Rodrigo himself was reluctant to frame what he was experiencing as a psychological problem. He came, he said, because his wife asked him to.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rodrigo was working late in the county evidence processing facility when a gas main beneath the building ruptured. The explosion was not instantaneous — there was first a low, building vibration that Rodrigo initially attributed to a truck on the adjacent highway, then the smell of something chemical and wrong, and then a pressure wave that threw him from his workstation and collapsed a section of the ceiling onto the lab. He was trapped for nearly two hours in a partially destroyed room, surrounded by structural debris, chemical fumes from compromised evidence containers, and the intermittent sounds of secondary structural failures somewhere deeper in the building. Two colleagues were seriously injured. Rodrigo sustained a broken wrist and lacerations but was able to move, which he later came to see as the source of a particular shame — he had stayed low and still, waiting for rescue, rather than attempting to reach his colleagues. He had not known where they were. He had not known what was still structurally sound. He had made the calculation that movement might cause further collapse. But in the months that followed, he had found it increasingly difficult to trust that calculation.

In the weeks after the explosion, Rodrigo returned to work on modified duties while his wrist healed. The lab had been relocated to a temporary facility in a part of the city he did not know well. It was there that something shifted. The unfamiliar corridors, the new floor plan, the exits he had not yet memorized — all of it produced a low, persistent vigilance that never fully released. He had come to believe, with a quiet but firm conviction, that the ability to read a space — to know its exits, its structural logic, its risks — was the only thing standing between a person and catastrophe. In an environment he could not yet read, his body simply refused to stand down. His shoulders ached by midday. He startled badly when a cabinet door slammed, or when a colleague appeared in his peripheral vision without announcement. The jumpiness embarrassed him, and the embarrassment compounded into something heavier.

What troubled Rodrigo most, perhaps, was not the vigilance itself but what he had concluded it meant. He had spent thirty years analyzing evidence with precision and composure, and he had always understood himself as someone who could function under pressure. The fact that he now flinched at ordinary sounds, that he found himself standing in the doorway of the new lab's break room unable to make himself enter because he had not yet identified all the exits — this, to him, was proof of something irreversible. He was certain that the man he had been before the explosion, the one who could walk into any scene and think clearly, was no longer available to him. He had also come to feel, in a way that permeated his thinking about the world beyond the lab, that danger was simply the baseline condition of existence — that he had been naive before, and that what he felt now was simply accurate perception rather than distortion.

Over the following months, Rodrigo began declining assignments that required site visits to unfamiliar locations. He offered procedural justifications each time, and for a while his supervisor accepted them. But the pattern accumulated, and three months ago he was passed over for a senior case lead he had been informally promised. His wife noticed that he no longer suggested they try new restaurants or visit friends in neighborhoods he did not know. She did not push, but her quiet accommodation of his new geography of safety was, in its own way, a measure of how much had changed.

What finally brought him in was a conversation with his wife in which she said, simply, that she missed him. He did not know how to respond to that. He hopes, cautiously, that something can be recovered. He is afraid that nothing can.
